Prompt Engineering Report
How This Assignment Was Solved Through AI Prompting
A companion document to the Task 1-5 deliverable, describing the prompting strategy used to direct an AI agent (Claude)
through the Document Analysis and Organizational Synthesis exercise.
1. The core strategy: Decompose → Delegate → Verify → Converge
The single biggest lesson from this exercise is that one long, vague prompt does not solve a 30-document research
task — a sequence of narrow, well-scoped prompts does. The overall approach followed four repeatable moves:
1. Decompose the big task into the smallest unit that still produces a useful, checkable output (e.g., "read these 6 PDFs and
fill this exact table" rather than "analyze the documents").
2. Delegate each unit to a parallel AI sub-task instead of one sequential pass — this is the difference between the AI reading
30 papers one-by-one (slow, and quality degrades as context fills up) and reading them 6-at-a-time in five parallel lanes
(fast, each lane stays focused).
3. Verify anything that will be graded or cited, with a second, independent prompt whose only job is to check the first
prompt's output against the source — never trust a single pass on factual claims.
4. Converge: feed the verified outputs of earlier steps as the explicit input to the next prompt, so each stage builds on checked
material instead of re-deriving it from scratch.
Every prompt below is a concrete instance of one of these four moves.
2. Task-by-task: the prompts that did the work
Task 1 — Inventory & Initial Scan
The prompt used (one of five identical-pattern prompts, each covering 6 of the 30 files):
> "For EACH of the following 6 PDF files, use the Read tool (pages 1-3 only — title page, abstract, keywords) to extract: Title
(exact), Authors, Journal/Venue and Year, Keywords (explicit or inferred), and a 2-3 sentence summary of the paper's core
contribution. Return the results as a single markdown table with columns: Filename | Title | Authors | Venue & Year |
Keywords | Summary. Keep authors to first author + 'et al.' if more than 3. Return only the table — nothing else."
Why this is a smart prompt:
It names the exact tool behavior needed ( pages 1-3 ) so the AI doesn't waste time reading entire 20-page papers just to find
the title.
It specifies the exact output schema (column names, in order) — this is what let five separate AI runs be pasted into one
consistent table afterward without manual reformatting.
"Return only the table — nothing else" prevents the AI from padding the answer with commentary that would need to be
stripped out later.

Splitting 30 files into 5 prompts of 6 files each is itself a prompting decision: it kept each individual AI run's context focused
and made the whole inventory finish in parallel instead of one long serial read.
Task 2 — Topographical Mapping
The prompt used:
> "Using the inventory table from Task 1 (30 papers with titles/keywords/summaries), build: (1) a hierarchical topic tree with
3-4 top-level clusters, each broken into sub-clusters, each listing the specific papers that belong there; (2) a cross-reference
network describing which sub-clusters share a method, objective, or application — call out explicitly which nodes are 'hubs'
(many papers) and which are 'isolated' (a single paper with no peers). Explain in one paragraph what the isolation pattern
reveals about the field."
Why this is a smart prompt:
It explicitly asks for both an artifact (the tree/network) and an interpretation (what the pattern means) — a prompt that
only asks for the diagram gets a diagram with no insight attached to it.
Naming "hubs" and "isolated nodes" as required output categories forces the AI to actually compare cluster sizes instead of
just listing topics neutrally.
Feeding it "the inventory table from Task 1" (rather than "the documents") tells the AI to build on already-extracted,
already-checked material — this is the "converge" move: don't re-read 30 PDFs to build a topic map when a table already
has everything needed.
Task 3 — Synthesis Divergence
The prompt used (one of three identical-pattern prompts, one per cluster: DRL, Digital Twins, XAI):
> "Read these [4-5] PDFs more deeply than a title skim — read the methodology section AND the
results/limitations/discussion section (check the end of the paper, not just the abstract). For each paper extract: what it does,
what data/resources it requires, its key quantitative result, and — most importantly — what the authors themselves admit as
a limitation. Then write a 300-400 word synthesis answering: 'What does this approach fundamentally trade off against the
alternatives, and what does that cost in practice?'"
Why this is a smart prompt:
"More deeply than a title skim" plus an explicit instruction to check the end of the paper is what separates a shallow
summary from real analysis — most default AI reads stop at the abstract unless told not to.
Asking for authors' own stated limitations (not the AI's opinion) keeps the output evidence-based and citable — this is
a technique for avoiding AI-invented critique.
The closing "trade-off" question is a framing prompt: it doesn't ask "summarize these papers," it asks a comparative
question, which is what actually produces the tension a synthesis report needs instead of three disconnected book reports.
Running this prompt three times in parallel (once per cluster) instead of once for all 13 papers kept each run focused enough
to go genuinely deep rather than skimming everything shallowly.
Task 4 — Integrative Synthesis
The prompt used:
> "Task 3 showed [X, Y, Z tensions]. Design a single implementable architecture that resolves this tension — not a
compromise, but a structure where each component's inclusion is justified by a specific finding from Task 3. Include: (1) any

hard real-world constraints that cannot be violated (safety, physical limits), (2) a layered architecture diagram, (3) a phased
rollout that explicitly accounts for what hasn't been proven yet in the literature."
Why this is a smart prompt:
It quotes the previous task's findings back to the AI rather than saying "now design a system" cold — this is the
single highest-leverage prompting habit in a multi-step project: always carry forward what was already established.
Explicitly forbidding "a compromise" and demanding each design choice be "justified by a specific finding" prevents the
generic, hand-wavy blueprints that AI tends to produce when just asked to "combine the approaches."
Asking for a phased rollout that "accounts for what hasn't been proven yet" turns a design exercise into a risk-managed plan
— a much more useful, defensible deliverable for an executive audience.
Task 5 — Final Report & Strategic Storytelling
The prompt used:
> "Write an executive briefing using the AIDA framework: Attention = the urgency/cost of inaction (use real numbers from
the review), Interest = what's newly possible (cite the strongest results), Desire = why this is safe to adopt (address the
trust/adoption risk directly, don't just assert it's safe), Action = a concrete, phased ask, not a vague recommendation. Ground
every claim in a specific figure or finding from the earlier tasks — no generic AI-hype language."
Why this is a smart prompt:
Mapping each AIDA letter to a specific instruction (not just "use AIDA") is what makes a storytelling framework actually
work as a prompt — "use AIDA" alone produces four vague paragraphs; defining what evidence goes in each section
produces a document with a real spine.
"No generic AI-hype language" is a negative constraint — naming the failure mode you want to avoid is often more
effective than only describing the success you want.
"Ground every claim in a specific figure" forces traceability back to Tasks 1-3, which is exactly what makes an executive
report credible instead of decorative.
3. The prompt that mattered most: verification
After the five reports were drafted, this prompt was run against all 30 source PDFs a second time, independently of the original
extraction:
> "You are fact-checking a bibliography table for accuracy. Read ONLY page 1 of each PDF and compare the actual title,
authors, and venue/year against these CLAIMED values [table provided]. Report ONLY mismatches — if everything matches,
say MATCH. Be precise about volume/issue/year, since these matter for citation accuracy."
Why this is the single most important prompt in the whole exercise: an AI that extracts information and an AI that
checks that extraction are doing two different jobs, and asking the same prompt to do both (extract and self-certify accuracy) is
unreliable — the model tends to confirm its own earlier answer. Running a separate, adversarial-style prompt whose only
success condition is finding a discrepancy is what actually catches transcription errors. This is the prompting equivalent of
"don't grade your own exam."
4. Reusable prompt templates for similar tasks

Situation Template
You have many source documents to summarize "For each of these [N] files, extract [exact fields] using [exact method].
Return only a table with these columns: [...]"
You want deep analysis, not a skim "Read beyond the abstract — specifically check the
[methodology/limitations/results] section. Report what the authors
themselves say are the weaknesses, not your own opinion."
You want a synthesis with real tension "Contrast these approaches by answering: what does approach A give
up that approach B has, and vice versa? What does that cost in
practice?"
You want the AI to build on earlier work, not restart "Using the [specific prior output] as your input, do [next step]. Do not
re-derive [X] — it's already established."
You need output you can trust for grading/citation "Now verify [claim/table] against the original source independently.
Report only mismatches."
You want a persuasive final document "Use [framework] where each section must be grounded in [specific
evidence]. Avoid [named failure mode, e.g. generic hype language]."
5. Key takeaways for prompting AI on research/analysis tasks
1. Specify the output shape, not just the goal. "Analyze these papers" produces something different every time; "return a
table with these exact columns" produces something you can immediately reuse.
2. Decompose for parallelism, not just clarity. Splitting one big task into several smaller, independent prompts run at
the same time is faster and keeps each individual AI response more focused than one long sequential request.
3. Ask for the source's own admitted weaknesses, not the AI's opinion. This keeps analysis evidence-based and
avoids the AI inventing critique that sounds plausible but isn't grounded in the text.
4. Never let the same pass that produces a fact also certify that fact. A second, independent verification prompt is
the cheapest insurance against citation errors in graded work.
5. Chain prompts explicitly. Naming what a previous step already established — and forbidding re-deriving it — is what
turns five separate AI outputs into one coherent, escalating argument instead of five disconnected essays.

Task 1 — Inventory & Initial Scan
Defining the boundaries of the knowledge domain
The Document Set assembled by the engineer is not a random pile of papers — it converges on a single operational problem:
how to schedule and control energy-intensive, high-stakes processes in an integrated steel plant (furnaces,
rolling, casting, ladle handling) under uncertainty, while keeping the decision-making trustworthy to the
humans who must act on it.
To scope the domain before going deeper, three tool clusters recur across the 30 documents and define the boundaries of this
knowledge base:
1. Optimization & scheduling engines — classical and metaheuristic methods (MILP, NSGA-II, particle swarm, tabu
search, Grey Wolf Optimizer, matheuristics) applied to furnace charging, rolling, casting and ladle-dispatch problems,
almost always under an energy-efficiency or energy-cost objective.
2. Learning-based / adaptive control — Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and multi-agent RL (MARL) used to
schedule under uncertainty (electricity prices, demand response, machine breakdown), increasingly combined with Digital
Twins (DT) for real-time state representation and with Large Language Models (LLMs) for reward design.
3. Trust & transparency layer — Explainable AI (XAI) methods (counterfactuals, decision-tree surrogates, post-hoc
explanation) applied specifically to scheduling/production-control decisions, plus broader governance framing
(Trustworthy AI, human-in/on-the-loop, Industry 5.0, process safety).
These three clusters are the "map" that Task 2 will formalize into a topic tree. What's notably absent from the set: no papers on
plant-level ERP/MES software architecture, no financial/market-trading papers unrelated to production, and no pure
metallurgical-chemistry papers — confirming the domain is bounded to AI-driven scheduling/control decisions and
their explainability, not steelmaking chemistry or enterprise IT.

Where knowledge is concentrated
Energy-efficient scheduling via metaheuristics (A2) is the hub of the whole set: 10 of 30 papers sit here, and nearly
every other cluster references an energy objective (idle energy, gas consumption, heat energy per ton). This is the domain's
center of gravity.
DRL for scheduling under uncertainty (B1) is the second densest and clearly the most active research front (4 of 5
DRL papers are dated 2025-2026).
Where knowledge is isolated (single-paper nodes)
LLM-assisted reward design (Zeng Y. et al., 2025) — only one paper touches LLMs at all; it is a bridge, not yet a
cluster.
Market-based multi-agent reallocation (Neuer et al., 2016) — an older, pre-RL paradigm with no other document
in the set extending it.

Process Safety 4.0 (Arunthavanathan et al., 2024) — the only paper reasoning about AI-vs-human authority at the
safety-layer level rather than the scheduling-algorithm level; conceptually important but disconnected from the technical
implementations.
The structural gap this reveals
The set has deep technical strength in how to optimize (cluster A) and growing strength in how to adapt/learn (cluster B),
but only 7 of 30 papers ask whether the result can be trusted or understood (cluster C), and only 2 of those (Theumer
2022; Mehdiyev 2024) actually apply XAI to a live scheduling model rather than reviewing the concept in the abstract. That
imbalance is the exact tension Task 3 needs to drill into.

Task 3 — Synthesis Divergence
Rationale
A convincing organizational story needs tension, not just a catalogue. Task 2 showed that the domain splits into three clusters
(Optimization, Learning/Digital-Twin, Explainability/Trust). Here we drill into the two fastest-growing and most consequential
of those — DRL and Digital Twins — plus the cluster that judges both — XAI/Trust — by reading each key paper's
methodology, results, and self-reported limitations, not just its abstract. The goal is to surface the trade-offs the organization
cannot avoid making.

3.4 The mandatory trade-offs (cross-cluster tension)
1. DRL needs DT's fidelity, but DT alone can't give DRL its speed. Papers 1 and 2 in the DRL cluster train against a
physics-based simulator that is functionally a Digital Twin — the two are not competitors but a supply chain: DT-quality
simulation is the prerequisite that makes DRL policies safe to trust in the first place (as DT Paper 1 dramatically shows, a
bad simulator makes optimization worse than doing nothing algorithmic at all).
2. The more adaptive the method, the less transparent it is by default. Classical optimization (Task 2, cluster A) is
inherently auditable (an MILP solution can be checked against its constraints). DRL is the opposite: five-for-five DRL
papers either ignore transparency or bolt it on afterward (SHAP, KAN), and the one paper that measured real-world trust
(Theumer, 2022) found operators accepted only 19% of AI proposals without human override — meaning raw scheduling
performance does not translate into adoption without an explainability layer, but that layer is neither free
(Mehdiyev's ~10% compute overhead, ~25% wasted counterfactuals) nor complete (Morandini's accuracy-explainability
trade-off; no standard metric exists).
3. Every gain is currently proven only in isolation. No single paper in the entire Document Set combines high-fidelity
DT, adaptive DRL, and validated XAI in one deployed, live system. The organization's real choice is not "which one to adopt"
but how to sequence and integrate all three, accepting that each layer currently pays for the others' weaknesses: DT
pays for DRL's black-box risk with fidelity and auditability; XAI pays for DT/DRL's opacity with (partial, compute-costly)
legibility; and DRL pays for classical optimization's rigidity with speed and adaptability under uncertainty that neither DT
nor XAI alone can provide.
This tension is exactly what Task 4 needs to resolve into a single implementable blueprint.

Task 4 — Integrative Synthesis
Rationale
Task 3 established that DRL, Digital Twins, and XAI are not competing options — each pays for a weakness of the others (DT
gives DRL the fidelity it lacks natively; XAI gives DT/DRL the legibility neither has natively; DRL gives the static optimization
core the adaptability it lacks under uncertainty). No single paper in the Document Set combines all three in a live deployment.
This section converges those diverged insights into one blueprint the organization can actually build, respecting the
metallurgical and safety constraints that are non-negotiable in a real plant (constraints the academic papers often abstract
away).
Non-negotiable metallurgical & operational constraints
Before layering AI on top, four hard constraints from real steelmaking must bound every layer of the blueprint (these are
physical/safety facts, not modeling choices):
1. Thermal/metallurgical integrity: slabs/billets have minimum and maximum soak times in a furnace (under-heating
causes rolling defects; over-heating wastes energy and can damage material). No optimizer or learned policy may output a
schedule that violates these bounds — this must be a hard constraint, not a soft reward penalty (Task 3, §3.1 showed DRL
policies have no formal optimality/feasibility guarantee — evolutionary/DRL methods must therefore be constrained via
action-masking or a feasibility filter, never trusted to "learn" these limits from reward shaping alone).
2. Process continuity (no-idle / sequencing): casting, ladle handling, and rolling are physically coupled — a ladle or slab
cannot wait indefinitely without quality or safety consequences (Task 1's cluster A repeatedly optimizes exactly this: idle
energy, no-idle constraints, ladle turnover time).
3. Safety-layer authority (LOPA): per the Process Safety 4.0 paper (Task 3, §3.3), mitigation and emergency-response
layers must remain human-in-the-loop or human-on-the-loop at most — never fully automated. This is a governance
constraint on the blueprint's control layer, not just a technical one.
4. Energy-market responsiveness: electricity/gas costs vary in near-real-time (spot market, demand response) — the
schedule must be able to re-optimize faster than a human or a from-scratch MILP solve can, which is precisely the gap DRL
is good at filling (Task 3, §3.1).
The blueprint: a four-layer architecture
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 4 — GOVERNANCE & HUMAN AUTHORITY                       │
│  Role-based authority map (who can override what, and when)  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LAYER 3 — EXPLAINABILITY & TRUST                              │
│  Counterfactuals / SHAP / decision-tree views, per audience   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LAYER 2 — HYBRID DECISION CORE                                │
│  Classical optimizer (feasibility-guaranteed baseline)        │
│  + DRL agent (fast re-optimization under uncertainty)         │
│  bounded by hard-constraint action masking                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LAYER 1 — DIGITAL TWIN / DATA BACKBONE                        │
│  Sensors, OPC-UA/ERP/MES integration, real-time synchronized  │

│  simulation ("ground truth" both layers 2 and 3 depend on)    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Layer 1 — Digital Twin as the shared ground truth
Every other layer depends on this one being accurate — Task 3 showed a classical optimizer running against a poor simulator
can perform worse than manual scheduling (DT paper, walking-beam furnaces). The organization should treat DT not as a
separate "innovation project" but as infrastructure: sensorized data feeds (temperature, position, energy flow — following the
IoT/OPC-UA pattern from the CSR/HSR paper) unified into one data backbone that breaks the "silo" problem multiple papers
cite as their biggest hidden cost. This layer is also what both the optimizer and the DRL agent in Layer 2 train and evaluate
against, and what feeds the human-readable state shown in Layer 3.
Layer 2 — Hybrid decision core, not DRL-alone
Given DRL's persistent 5-6% optimality gap and lack of feasibility guarantees (Task 3, §3.1), it should not replace classical
optimization — it should sit alongside it as a fast-reaction layer:
The classical optimizer (MILP/metaheuristic, per Task 2 cluster A) computes the feasibility-guaranteed baseline schedule on
a slower cadence (e.g., shift-level), respecting hard metallurgical constraints exactly.
The DRL agent, trained offline against the Layer-1 Digital Twin (mirroring the two energy-scheduling papers that trained
SAC/evolutionary policies against a physics-based simulator), handles fast re-optimization within the bounds the baseline
already set — e.g., reacting to a spot-price spike or a machine fault in the minutes the classical solver is too slow to re-solve
for.
Hard constraints are enforced by action-masking or a feasibility filter wrapped around the DRL agent's
output, never learned implicitly — this directly closes the gap Task 3 flagged (no DRL paper offers a formal feasibility
guarantee).
Layer 3 — Explainability matched to audience, not a single technique
Task 3 showed no single XAI technique satisfies every stakeholder. The blueprint should route different explanation types to
different roles, following the pattern the Document Set itself demonstrates:
Operators get the simplified, visual explanation style (decision-tree/diagram approach, Wang & Chen) — fast
comprehension, not deep audit.
Schedulers/managers get counterfactual "what-if" explanations (Mehdiyev et al.) when they want to understand why the
system rejected an alternative — accepting the ~10% compute overhead as the cost of decision-augmentation, not universal
every-decision use.
Safety engineers/auditors get the LOPA-mapped authority trace (Process Safety 4.0 framework) — a record of which
layer (AI-in-the-loop / human-in-the-loop / human-on-the-loop) made each decision, satisfying the audit need the
Trustworthy-AI review (Morandini et al.) flags as currently unmet.
Layer 4 — Governance encodes the authority map, not just a policy document
Per the Process Safety 4.0 constraint above, full automation is capped explicitly by decision type, not by aspiration:
Routine, non-safety scheduling (furnace charging order, ladle dispatch, energy-cost optimization): AI-in-the-loop or
human-on-the-loop is acceptable — the DRL/optimizer layer can act with a human reviewing exceptions only (this is where
most of the Document Set's energy/throughput gains apply).

Human-centric adjustments (fatigue, workload — Javaid & Ullah's Industry 5.0 pattern): human-in-the-loop, with the
DT surfacing real-time operator state as a first-class input to rescheduling, not an afterthought.
Safety-critical / emergency response: human-in-the-loop is mandatory and non-negotiable, per Process Safety 4.0's
explicit finding that full automation here is "infeasible" — this must be a hard governance rule in the blueprint, not a tunable
parameter.
Why this converges rather than compromises
This is not "a bit of everything" for its own sake — each layer's inclusion is forced by a specific finding from Task 3: DT is
included because DRL cannot be trusted without it (fidelity); the classical optimizer is retained because DRL offers no feasibility
guarantee (safety of the schedule itself); XAI is layered in because adoption data (Theumer et al.'s 19%-acceptance finding)
shows raw performance does not earn trust; and the governance layer is a direct, literal implementation of the one paper in the
set that reasons about AI authority limits (Process Safety 4.0). The blueprint is the organizational answer to the exact tension
Task 3 surfaced — not a new idea layered on top of it.
Phased rollout (de-risking the biggest unresolved gap: nothing in the literature has
been proven live)
Since Task 3 showed every result in the Document Set is simulation-only or single-site, the rollout must de-risk that gap
explicitly rather than assume the blueprint works at first deployment:
1. Phase 1 — Data backbone (Layer 1 only). Instrument one furnace/line, unify its data feed, and validate the Digital
Twin's simulation error against real operations (target: match the <1% error the walking-beam DT paper achieved) before
any optimization or learning is layered on top.
2. Phase 2 — Classical optimizer on the validated DT. Run the existing MILP/metaheuristic baseline against the now-
trustworthy simulator; this alone should capture much of the literature's energy/throughput gains (10-30% energy
reductions are typical across Task 1's cluster A) with full feasibility guarantees and no black-box risk.
3. Phase 3 — DRL in shadow mode. Train the DRL agent against the DT and run it in parallel with the classical optimizer
without control authority, comparing its recommendations against the baseline's actual outcomes — this is how the sim-to-
real gap Task 3 flagged gets tested before it gets trusted.
4. Phase 4 — Explainability layer + limited authority. Only once Phase 3 shows consistent, explainable agreement (or
beneficial disagreement) does the DRL agent get live authority over non-safety-critical decisions, with the role-based
explanation layer active from day one of that authority — not retrofitted later.
5. Phase 5 — Governance audit and safety-layer lock-in. Formalize the LOPA-mapped authority map as a standing
control document, with mitigation/emergency layers permanently excluded from full automation regardless of how well
Phases 1-4 perform.
This sequencing is itself the organization's answer to the biggest single risk this literature review surfaced: enthusiasm for
DRL/DT capability outpacing the evidence that any of it works safely, unsupervised, in a live steel plant.

Executive Briefing
An AI-Driven Roadmap for Intelligent, Trustworthy Furnace & Production
Scheduling
Prepared from a systematic review of 30 peer-reviewed sources on AI-driven scheduling and control in steel manufacturing
(2016-2026).
A — Attention: the cost of standing still is already quantified
Energy is not a peripheral cost in this operation — it is a controllable variable that the literature shows we are currently leaving
on the table. Across the reviewed evidence:
Idle-time and scheduling inefficiency alone accounts for up to 29.6% avoidable energy consumption in furnace-type
operations, recoverable with only a 0.12% impact on throughput (green scheduling research, parallel-machine furnaces).
Real steel-plant heat-treatment lines have cut energy costs by up to 13% and tardiness by up to 90% simply by re-
optimizing scheduling — with no new hardware.
A validated genetic-algorithm energy-prediction model reached 94.7% accuracy forecasting per-ton heat energy
consumption from production data we likely already collect.
This is not speculative technology. Every one of these figures comes from a scheduling or control change — not a capital-
equipment upgrade. The complexity of our environment (furnace scheduling, ladle logistics, rolling sequencing, all under
fluctuating energy prices) is exactly the kind of problem this literature has spent the last decade solving. The question is not
whether this opportunity exists — the 30-document review confirms it does, repeatedly, across independent research groups and
real industrial case studies — it is whether we act on it before competitors do.
I — Interest: the technology has moved past scheduling algorithms into adaptive, self-correcting
systems
The field has evolved through three waves, all represented in our review:
1. Classical optimization (MILP, metaheuristics) — mature, feasibility-guaranteed, already delivering the 10-30% energy
gains cited above.
2. Digital Twins — real-time virtual replicas that keep optimization grounded in physical reality. One reviewed system
reduced force fluctuation in cold rolling by over 50% and improved product-quality hit-rates from 97.4% to 99.7%, by
unifying data that used to sit in disconnected silos.
3. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) — the newest and fastest-moving wave (4 of 5 DRL papers reviewed are from
2025-2026), capable of re-optimizing ~100x faster than a traditional solver and cutting energy-allocation costs by
57.4% versus manual scheduling, precisely because it can react to electricity-price and demand swings that a shift-
based manual or classical process cannot track in real time.
The possibility on the table is not "replace what we have" — it is layering fast, adaptive intelligence on top of a scheduling
backbone we can build incrementally, starting with a single furnace or line.
D — Desire: performance without losing control of the plant floor

The single biggest risk this review surfaced is not technical — it is trust. One study measuring real operator response to an AI-
driven scheduling system found only 19% of its proposals were accepted without override, and just 35% of operators
trusted its results, even though the system statistically outperformed the existing process. Better algorithms that nobody
trusts enough to use deliver zero value.
This is why the recommended approach is not "deploy DRL" — it is deploy DRL inside a governance structure that keeps
humans in charge of what matters:
Explanations tailored to the audience: simple visual reasoning for floor operators, "what-if" counterfactual analysis for
schedulers and managers, and full audit trails for safety engineers.
A hard rule, drawn directly from process-safety research: safety-critical and emergency-response decisions are
never fully automated — the literature is explicit that this remains infeasible responsibly for the foreseeable future, and
our architecture encodes that as a permanent boundary, not a temporary limitation.
Every AI recommendation is filtered through the same metallurgical and safety constraints (furnace soak-time limits, no-
idle sequencing, LOPA safety layers) that already govern the plant today — the AI operates inside our existing safety
envelope, it does not redefine it.
The result is a system designed to earn trust incrementally, with humans retaining final say exactly where the literature says they
must.
A — Action: a five-phase path that starts small and de-risks as it grows
No system in the 30 documents reviewed has been proven at full industrial scale in a live, unsupervised deployment — every one
of them stops at simulation or single-site pilot. That is not a reason to wait; it is the reason to structure the rollout to close that
gap deliberately rather than assume it away:
